In that paper prilocaine was compared with mepivacaine and aptocaine in the same subjects; lignocaine was injected in a separate earlier trial in a different group of 28 volunteers.

proposed_wording: Head-to-head duration figures in minutes on a skin endpoint exist in humans as well as in horses. Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) timed prilocaine against mepivacaine and aptocaine by pinprick over an intradermal bleb in the same 27 human volunteers, reporting 32 min to 50% recovery for prilocaine against 60 min for the other two, and mean times to full recovery of 78.6, 98.6 and 98.9 min. The horse study (Harcourt 2021, PMID 34569052) is still the only one reporting means with confidence intervals, and the only one using a mechanical nociceptive threshold after a palmar digital nerve block.
reason: The full text gives duration in minutes for every agent in both trials, by two endpoints: time to 50% recovery read from the mean recovery curves, and mean time to full recovery tabulated in minutes with SEM. So Reynolds 1976 is a human head-to-head skin measurement in minutes, not merely a ranking. Prilocaine 1, 2 and 3% was compared with mepivacaine 1, 2 and 3% and aptocaine 1%, all at 0.1 ml intradermally, in the same 27 volunteers in one session, which matches every element the claim says is absent, including 'any species'. The horse study is therefore not the only head-to-head duration measurement in minutes on a skin endpoint, although it remains the only one with confidence intervals.

Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) timed plain bupivacaine to full recovery at a wheal volume in 28 double-blind volunteers, mean 82.5 min, alongside lignocaine at 65.7 min, and in a second trial of 27 volunteers timed mepivacaine (98.6 min pooled) and prilocaine (78.6 min pooled) by the same endpoint. Ropivacaine has been timed to full return of sensation only at a larger intradermal volume (Moffitt 2001, PMID 11359489), and articaine has not been timed in human skin. Every wheal-volume figure so far is under two hours.

For bupivacaine 0.5% that gives 82.5 +/- 8.7 min in 28 volunteers, and in the second trial mepivacaine 1, 2 and 3% gives 98.6 +/- 4.7 min and prilocaine 1, 2 and 3% gives 78.6 +/- 5.1 min pooled in 27 volunteers. Bupivacaine therefore matches every element the claim says is absent, including 'at a wheal volume', so the count of four fails and bupivacaine joins the drugs timed to complete recovery at a wheal volume; articaine remains untimed in skin and ropivacaine's only full-recovery figure is still at a larger volume.

proposed_wording: No source was found for a 2.5-hour mepivacaine duration in skin, and at least four human studies have timed mepivacaine in skin (Reynolds 1976, PMID 776194; Fairley 1981; Willatts 1985; Christoph 1988), not two. The earliest, Reynolds 1976, timed intradermal mepivacaine at three concentrations in 27 double-blind volunteers by pinprick over the bleb: mean times to full recovery of 97.0, 95.2 and 103.7 min, 98.6 min pooled (n=81), and 60 min to 50% recovery. The longest of those means is about 1.7 h, and duration did not rise with concentration.

The substance of the claim - no source for 2.5 hours, and the measured skin durations far below it - therefore holds, but the count of studies does not.
